values.value: MCP turns your AI from a talker into a doer
The Model Context Protocol lets AI assistants use real tools. Here is why that changes what they can do for you.
An AI that can only chat is a clever pen pal. Give it MCP and it can actually open the tools you work in — and get things done.

value.markup:
For years, talking to an AI meant copying and pasting. You described your problem, the model described a solution, and you went off to carry it out by hand. The conversation was smart, but the hands were yours.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) changes that. It is an open standard that lets an AI assistant discover and call tools exposed by other software — a database, a ticketing system, a file system, or a CMS — through one consistent interface.

values.value: Tools, connected. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.

value.markup:
From describing to doing

This very blog is a good example. Every document type, every block, every image and every word on this site was created by an AI assistant calling the Umbraco MCP server — no clicking through the backoffice, no hand-written migrations.

  • It inspected the existing document types and data types before changing anything.
  • It modeled the content: element types for blocks, a block grid for the page body.
  • It imported the media and published the content, then read it back to confirm it landed.

The assistant did not need a bespoke plugin for any of that. It simply asked the server what tools were available and used them.

values.value: An assistant that can only talk is a consultant. An assistant that can act is a colleague.

values.value: MCP is a single open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools, replacing a tangle of one-off integrations.
Without a standard, every AI-to-tool connection is a custom job. MCP replaces the tangle with a single plug that fits everything.

value.markup:
Before USB, every device came with its own cable and its own port. Connecting an AI to your tools has looked much the same: one custom integration per assistant, per tool, each maintained separately and each breaking in its own way.

MCP is the USB port for AI. A tool author writes one MCP server; any MCP-capable assistant can use it. An assistant implements one MCP client; it can talk to every server out there.

values.value: Write the integration once. Use it from every assistant.
The whole point of a standard
Standard connections beat bespoke wiring. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Why that is awesome

  • Discoverable. The server tells the assistant what it can do, with typed inputs and descriptions. Nothing is hard-coded into the prompt.
  • Local and private. The Umbraco MCP server runs on your machine, next to your dev site, using a scoped API user.
  • Composable. Add a second server — version control, a browser, a database — and the same assistant can combine them in one task.
  • Future-proof. Swap the assistant or upgrade the tool; the contract in the middle stays the same.

That is a lot of leverage for a small, boring protocol — which is exactly what good standards are.
